parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State a similarity and a difference between an up quark and an up antiquark.

markscheme_points.text: similarity: same/equal mass or same/equal (magnitude of) charge or both fundamental (particles)
difference: opposite (sign of) charge or one is matter and the other is antimatter

hints: Hint 1: Think about what defines a particle and its antiparticle - which properties must stay exactly the same for them to be a pair?
Hint 2: Now think about charge: an up quark has charge $+2/3e$. What must the sign be for its antiparticle, and what word describes matter versus antimatter?
parts.proper_answer: similarity: same (rest) mass and same magnitude of charge (both are fundamental particles). difference: opposite sign of charge (+2/3e for up quark, -2/3e for up antiquark) - one is matter, the other is antimatter.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What an antiparticle keeps the same**
Think of an antiparticle as a mirror twin. It has exactly the same rest mass as the particle, and the same size of charge. Both the up quark and up antiquark are fundamental particles, so they cannot be broken down further.

Step 2: **What an antiparticle reverses**
The key change is the sign of all charges. An up quark has charge $$Q = +\frac{2}{3}e$$ so the up antiquark has $$Q = -\frac{2}{3}e$$ One is matter and the other is antimatter, so they would annihilate if they met.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Fig. 7.1 shows an electron in an electric field, in a vacuum, at an instant when the electron is stationary.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 7.1, draw an arrow to show the direction of the electric force acting on the stationary electron.
hints: Hint 1: Recall which way field lines point relative to force on a positive charge, then ask yourself what changes because an electron is negative.
parts.proper_answer: Arrow drawn at the electron pointing to the right, opposite to the field lines.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Force direction for a negative charge**
By definition, electric field direction is the direction of force on a positive charge. The field lines in Fig. 7.1 point to the left. An electron has negative charge, so the force on it is opposite to the field: $$\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$$ with $q$ negative. So starting at the electron dot, draw a short straight arrow to the right.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The electric field causes the electron to move from its initial position.

Describe and explain the acceleration of the electron due to the field, as the electron moves through the field.

markscheme_points.text: (electric) field strength increases or (electric) force increases

hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the spacing of the field lines to the right of the electron, where it is about to move - are the lines getting closer together or further apart?
Hint 2: Link line spacing to field strength to force to acceleration using $F = EQ$ and $F = ma$ with constant $Q$ and $m$.
parts.proper_answer: Acceleration increases. The field lines converge / get closer together in the direction of motion (to the right), so electric field strength $E$ increases, so electric force $F = EQ$ increases, so $a = F/m$ increases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the field pattern**
Closer field lines mean a stronger field. In Fig. 7.1 the lines are further apart on the left and closer together on the right. From (b)(i) the electron is pushed to the right, so it moves into a region where the lines are closer.

Step 2: **From stronger field to larger acceleration**
A stronger field means a larger force on the same charge: $$F = EQ$$ The electron charge $Q = -e$ has constant magnitude and its mass $m$ is constant, so Newton's second law gives: $$a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{EQ}{m}$$ As $E$ increases, $F$ increases and therefore $a$ increases. So the electron accelerates more and more to the right.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
A stationary $\alpha$-particle is now placed in the same electric field at the same initial position that was occupied by the electron.

Compare the initial electric force acting on the $\alpha$-particle with the initial electric force that acted on the electron.

markscheme_points.text: force (on α-particle) has twice the magnitude
force (on α-particle) is in opposite direction

hints: Hint 1: Compare the charges that go into $F = EQ$ - what is the charge of an electron and what is the charge of an alpha-particle in terms of $e$?
Hint 2: Think separately about size and direction: how does the size of $|Q|$ affect the size of $F$, and how does the sign of $Q$ affect the direction relative to the field?
parts.proper_answer: Force on alpha-particle is twice the magnitude of force on electron and in the opposite direction (to the left, along the field).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare the charges**
At the same position $E$ is the same. Electron charge is $$Q_e = -e$$ Alpha-particle (helium nucleus, 2 protons) charge is $$Q_{\alpha} = +2e$$ So the magnitude $|Q|$ is twice as large for the alpha-particle.

Step 2: **Apply F = EQ for size and direction**
Magnitude: $$|F| = |Q|E$$ so $$|F_{\alpha}| = 2eE = 2|F_e|$$ The force is twice as large. Direction: positive charge is pushed along $E$ (to the left), negative charge opposite to $E$ (to the right). So the alpha-particle force is opposite in direction to the electron force.
